newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: KLM, Northwest seal billion dollar peace pact.
newsitem.headline: KLM, Northwest seal billion dollar peace pact.

text.p: Dutch carrier KLM said Wednesday it agreed to sell its 19 percent stake in Northwest Airlines back to the U.S. carrier in a billion-dollar deal aimed at strengthening their lucrative but often stormy alliance.
KLM will sell back its holding to Northwest in four annual tranches at a total price of $1.07 billiion to $1.17 billion in exchange for a long-term cooperation deal.

The deal, hailed by industry analysts as a welcome resolution to the airlines' lengthy boardroom battle over control of Northwest, could create "the most far-reaching airline alliance ever seen," the carriers said in a joint statement.
Northwest's stock jumped on the news, gaining $1.625 to $39.75 in early trading on Nasdaq.

The airlines said they committed themselves to a commercial and operational relationship for a minimum of 10 years, building further strategies for joint marketing and product development and extending their alliance by bringing in new partners.
Analysts said the agreement heralded a new phase in the relationship, adding that KLM's top priority now was to seek a European partner.
"The most important thing now is to pick up a European partner to boost their market share to the targeted 15 percent," said Frits de Vries, airlines analyst with Gilissen Bankiers.
He said KLM's unambiguous decision to go ahead with Northwest ruled out the likelihood of a link-up with British Airways, currently awaiting EU approval for its mega tie-up with American Airlines .
Instead, KLM would likely seek ties with Italy's Alitalia, Northwest's preferred European partnership candidate, he said.
"They (Alitalia) have an estimated 6 percent share of the European market, which together with KLM's current 8 percent should bring them close to target," De Vries said.
Alitalia also has a strong position in Latin America, a blank spot in Northwest's route network, he added.
The Italian carrier's state holding company said earlier this week that KLM was at the top of its list for an alliance with the financially troubled carrier.
But KLM itself was tight-lipped on potential candidates.

"We never call names in that respect but the intention of both partners is to expand their alliances with other partners ... to come to a global airline system," KLM spokesman Peter Wellhuener told Reuters Financial Television.
The reinforced deal with Northwest was expected to boost operating profits, another spokesman told Reuters.
"The alliance currently generates around $150 million annually in terms of operating profits," Hans Leijte said. "This can only increase."
While the partnership -- the first-ever transatlantic alliance to gain U.S. anti-trust immunity -- has flourished at the level of operations, boardroom relations have been frosty.

The two airlines have bickered for several years, with KLM taking the U.S. carrier to court over a shareholder rights plan to prevent KLM gaining a further 5 percent stake under an option exercisable in 1998.
Northwest has repeatedly charged KLM with seeking to take it over, labelling the Dutch carrier a "creeping control threat."
The airlines said in their statement that they planned to finalise their agreement within 60 days and that KLM would subsequently withdraw pending legal actions.

Industry sources said the breakthrough could well have been prompted by the imminent change of leadership at KLM, although Leijte was quick to stress that outgoing Chief Executive Pieter Bouw had been instrumental in clinching the deal.
Leo van Wijk, currently KLM's chief operating officer, will take over the helm at KLM's annual general meeting on Aug. 5.

"The deal was likely eased by the arrival of Van Wijk," said one industry source. "Bouw took a very hard line in the past, and there were clear signs of a personality clash between him and Northwest executive John Dasburg."
